questions.stem: Dana's spouse died in 2024. Dana has not remarried and pays over half the cost of keeping up a home that is the principal residence of Dana's dependent child for all of 2026. Which filing status may Dana use for the 2026 tax return?
options: Single
Head of household
Qualifying surviving spouse
Married filing jointly
questions.explanation: Qualifying surviving spouse status is available for the two tax years following the year of a spouse's death (here, 2025 and 2026) if the taxpayer has not remarried, maintains a home that is the principal residence of a dependent child for the whole year, and paid over half the cost of keeping up that home. Head of household would apply once the two-year window has passed.

questions.stem: A married couple lives together all year and wants to file separate returns. If one spouse itemizes deductions on Form 1040, what is required of the other spouse?
options: The other spouse may freely choose to itemize or claim the standard deduction
The other spouse must also itemize, even if it produces a $0 itemized total
The other spouse must claim the standard deduction
The couple must instead file a joint return
questions.explanation: Under MFS, if one spouse itemizes, the other spouse's standard deduction is treated as zero — the other spouse must also itemize (even if that means claiming little or nothing), rather than being free to claim the standard deduction.

questions.stem: Which of the following, by itself, disqualifies a taxpayer from claiming head of household status?
options: Being unmarried at the end of the year
Paying more than half the cost of keeping up the home
Living with a qualifying person for more than half the year
Filing a joint return with a spouse for the year
questions.explanation: Head of household requires the taxpayer to be unmarried (or considered unmarried) at year end and to file their own return; filing a joint return with a spouse is fundamentally incompatible with claiming head of household for that year. The other three items are requirements, not disqualifiers.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's 20-year-old child lived at home all year, is not a full-time student, and earned $9,000 in wages that the child spent on personal expenses. The taxpayer provided the rest of the child's support. Can the taxpayer claim the child as a dependent?
options: Yes, as a qualifying child, because the child lived at home all year
No, because a 20-year-old who is not a full-time student fails the qualifying child age test and is tested instead as a qualifying relative
Yes, automatically, because the taxpayer provided most of the child's support
No, because the child's own earnings disqualify the taxpayer regardless of the test used
questions.explanation: The qualifying child age test caps at under 19, or under 24 only if a full-time student (or any age if permanently and totally disabled). A 20-year-old non-student fails that test, so the child can only be a dependent as a qualifying relative — which requires the child's gross income to be under the exemption-amount threshold for the year. $9,000 of wages would need to be checked against that threshold before concluding either way; the point tested here is which test applies, not an assumed outcome.

questions.stem: Divorced parents Casey and Jordan do not file a joint return. Their child lived with Casey for 210 nights and with Jordan for 155 nights during the year, and both parents otherwise meet the requirements to claim the child. Absent a signed release (Form 8332) to the contrary, which parent may claim the child as a qualifying child?
options: Jordan, because Jordan has the lower adjusted gross income
Casey, because the child resided with Casey for the greater number of nights
Whichever parent claims the child first on a timely filed return
Neither parent, because the child must be claimed by mutual written agreement
questions.explanation: The tiebreaker rule for divorced or separated parents who don't file jointly awards the qualifying child to the parent with whom the child resided the greater number of nights during the year. Adjusted gross income only becomes the tiebreaker if the nights are exactly equal.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's elderly parent does not live with the taxpayer but the taxpayer pays for more than half of the parent's total support and the parent's gross income is under the qualifying-relative threshold. What test does the parent NOT need to satisfy that a non-relative living in the home would?
options: The gross income test
The support test
The member-of-household-or-relationship test, as it applies to a member of household requirement
The joint return test
questions.explanation: A qualifying relative must either be related to the taxpayer in one of the specified ways or live with the taxpayer all year as a member of the household. A parent satisfies this through the relationship prong and, unlike an unrelated person, does not also need to live in the taxpayer's home to qualify.

questions.stem: A calendar-year individual taxpayer files Form 4868 by the original due date and it is accepted. What does this extension actually accomplish?
options: It extends both the time to file and the time to pay any tax owed
It extends the time to file the return but not the time to pay any tax owed
It extends the time to pay but requires the return to still be filed on the original due date
It waives any failure-to-pay penalty regardless of when the balance is paid
questions.explanation: Form 4868 grants an automatic extension of time to file (typically six months), but it does not extend the time to pay. Tax owed is still due by the original due date, and interest and the failure-to-pay penalty generally continue to accrue on any unpaid balance from that date.

questions.stem: A self-employed taxpayer has $500 of net self-employment earnings for the year and no other income. Which statement is correct about the filing requirement?
options: No return is required because total income is below the standard filing-threshold amounts
A return is required because net self-employment earnings of $400 or more trigger a filing requirement regardless of the general gross-income thresholds
A return is required only if the taxpayer also owes income tax on the amount
A return is required only if the taxpayer received a Form 1099-NEC for the income
questions.explanation: Net self-employment earnings of $400 or more create a filing requirement on their own, to capture self-employment tax, independent of the general gross-income filing thresholds that apply to wage and other income.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is claimed as a dependent on someone else's return and has only unearned income (interest and dividends) for the year. Compared to a taxpayer who is not claimed as a dependent, how is this dependent's own filing requirement determined?
options: Using the same gross-income thresholds that apply to non-dependents
Using separate, generally lower thresholds specific to dependents, based on earned and unearned income
There is never a filing requirement for a dependent regardless of income
Only the person who claims the dependent has any filing obligation related to that income
questions.explanation: A dependent's filing requirement is measured against its own set of thresholds (which differ for earned income, unearned income, and combinations of the two), not the general thresholds that apply to a taxpayer who isn't claimed as a dependent.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old dependent has $4,000 of interest income and no earned income for the year. Which statement about the kiddie tax rules is correct?
options: The kiddie tax cannot apply because the child is under 18
The kiddie tax can apply because the child is under 18 at year end, regardless of earned income
The kiddie tax only applies once the child turns 18
The kiddie tax applies only if the child files a joint return
questions.explanation: The kiddie tax age test is met for any child under age 18 at year end, without regard to how much earned income the child has. (The earned-income-versus-support comparison only comes into play for the 18, and 19–23 full-time student, age brackets.)

questions.stem: A 19-year-old, full-time college student who is a dependent has $6,000 of earned income and $3,000 of unearned income, and the earned income is more than half of the student's own support for the year. Does the kiddie tax apply?
options: Yes, because the student is under 24
No, because a full-time student age 19–23 is only subject to the kiddie tax if earned income does NOT exceed half of the student's own support, and here it does
Yes, because the student has any unearned income at all
No, full-time students are always exempt from the kiddie tax
questions.explanation: For the 19–23 full-time-student bracket, the kiddie tax age test is met only when the student's earned income does NOT exceed half of their own support. Because this student's earned income does exceed half of their support, the age test for this bracket is not met, so the kiddie tax does not apply on that basis.

questions.stem: Parents want to report their young child's interest and dividend income directly on their own return instead of filing a separate return for the child. Which form supports that election, and which form is used if the parents do not make it?
options: Form 8814 to elect to include the child's income on the parents' return; Form 8615 on the child's own return if the election is not made
Form 8615 to elect to include the child's income on the parents' return; Form 8814 on the child's own return if the election is not made
Form 8332 for either option, depending on custodial status
Schedule 8812 for either option, depending on the amount of income
questions.explanation: Form 8814 (Parents' Election to Report Child's Interest and Dividends) lets qualifying parents include the child's investment income on their own return. If the parents don't make that election — or the child doesn't qualify for it — the child's own return computes the kiddie tax using Form 8615.

questions.stem: For purposes of computing the premium tax credit, whose income generally makes up 'household income' on Form 8962?
options: Only the taxpayer's own modified AGI
The modified AGI of the taxpayer, the taxpayer's spouse if filing jointly, and any dependents who are required to file a return
The modified AGI of every person listed on the Marketplace application, regardless of filing requirement
Gross income before any adjustments, for the taxpayer and spouse only
questions.explanation: Household income for the premium tax credit is the taxpayer's modified AGI plus the modified AGI of the spouse (if filing jointly) and of each dependent who is required to file a tax return for the year — not every dependent regardless of filing requirement.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received advance premium tax credit payments during the year that turned out to exceed the premium tax credit actually allowed based on year-end income. What happens on the return?
options: The excess is always forgiven and requires no repayment
The excess advance payments are reconciled on Form 8962 and generally must be repaid, subject to any applicable repayment limitation based on income
The taxpayer must amend the Marketplace application instead of addressing it on the tax return
The excess is treated as an itemized deduction reduction with no other adjustment
questions.explanation: Form 8962 reconciles advance payments against the premium tax credit actually computed from year-end household income and family size. Excess advance payments generally must be repaid as additional tax, though the amount owed can be limited depending on income — the mechanics of that limitation are set by the current-year rules rather than fixed permanently in the statute.

questions.stem: Two separate tax families were both covered under a single Marketplace policy for part of the year (for example, divorced parents whose child is covered on one parent's policy while both parents are separate tax families). How is the premium tax credit computed for each family?
options: Only the policyholder may claim any premium tax credit for the policy
Each family computes its own credit independently with no allocation between them
The policy amounts (enrollment premium, applicable SLCSP premium, and advance payments) are allocated between the tax families, typically on Form 8962, Part IV
The premium tax credit is unavailable whenever more than one tax family is covered by the same policy
questions.explanation: When one Marketplace policy covers individuals from more than one tax family, the relevant policy amounts must be allocated between the families — commonly by an agreed percentage — using the shared policy allocation mechanics on Form 8962, rather than each family or only the policyholder claiming the credit unallocated.

questions.stem: Under the substantial presence test, which combination of facts, by itself, is sufficient to make a non-citizen a resident alien for the current year (absent an exception)?
options: Present in the U.S. for 20 days in the current year and 200 days in the prior year
Present in the U.S. for 40 days in the current year, with a weighted three-year total (current year plus one-third of the prior year plus one-sixth of the year before that) of at least 183 days
Present in the U.S. for any number of days in the current year, as long as the taxpayer holds a valid visa
Present in the U.S. for 100 days in the current year only, regardless of prior years
questions.explanation: The substantial presence test requires at least 31 days of presence in the current year AND a weighted total of at least 183 days across the current year (full weight), the prior year (one-third weight), and the year before that (one-sixth weight). A bare 20-day current-year count fails the 31-day threshold outright, no matter the weighted total.

questions.stem: A taxpayer was a nonresident alien for part of the year and became a resident alien partway through the same year, with no election to be treated differently. What best describes this taxpayer's filing position for that year?
options: The taxpayer files only Form 1040-NR for the entire year
The taxpayer files only Form 1040 for the entire year, exactly as a full-year resident would

The taxpayer is a dual-status alien for the year, generally reporting the resident period and nonresident period under their respective rules, with restrictions such as not using the standard deduction for the dual-status return
The taxpayer chooses freely which single return to file for the whole year with no restrictions
questions.explanation: A taxpayer who is a nonresident alien for part of the year and a resident alien for the rest is a dual-status alien. The return reflects both periods, and dual-status filers face specific restrictions — for example, they generally cannot claim the standard deduction — that don't apply to a taxpayer who was a resident alien for the full year.

questions.stem: An individual is not eligible for a Social Security number but needs a U.S. taxpayer identification number to be listed on a return, for example as a nonresident alien spouse. What is true of the ITIN issued in this situation?
options: It authorizes the holder to work legally in the United States
It establishes eligibility for the earned income tax credit
It confers a particular immigration status on the holder
It is issued solely for federal tax reporting purposes and does none of the above
questions.explanation: An ITIN is issued strictly to allow federal tax reporting for people who need a taxpayer identification number but aren't eligible for a Social Security number. It does not authorize work, does not by itself establish eligibility for the earned income tax credit (which requires a valid SSN), and does not confer or change immigration status.
